cells.tense: Right now you are tending the space between people, and your hands are steady.
cells.ask: Pick one person and say out loud what you are holding for them, plainly, once.
cells.core:
You're sitting with what someone else is feeling, and your hands are steady. You keep the space between you and them in good repair, and you know the small moves that do it — the pause, the question that lets a thing land. None of that needs an audience.

What you've built is real, and it runs quietly. The practice that keeps this reliable is the same practice that leaves you holding things alone in a room. There's one person on the list, or one thing left unsaid, waiting for you to bring it out. Say what you're holding for one person, plainly, before the week turns. That's not loosening the discipline — it's the discipline showing its face. It gives the quiet work a name someone can hear, and leaves you a little less to carry by yourself.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding it steady. Steady deserves a witness now and then.
cells.verb: holding space for what someone feels and tending the connection between you
cells.place: a long practice of turning intention into skill, kept by repetition

cells.tense: You are already bracing toward an ending and managing lives that have not arrived yet.
cells.ask: Name one ending you keep rehearsing, then leave it alone for a week.
cells.core:
You're running ahead of the room, feeling endings that haven't happened and getting there first. Before anyone has asked, before anything has actually ended, you've made the call and started preparing for it. Even ordinary conversation gets a little rehearsal.

What goes missing is the middle — the stretch where nothing has ended yet and people could still surprise you. The bracing has gotten out in front of the relationship it was meant to protect. Let one ending sit where it is for a week. Don't announce it, don't prepare for it, don't raise it. If the connection matters, it can survive seven days of you not managing it. What you're protecting and what you might actually be meeting are worth telling apart.
cells.sheetLine: You're halfway through an ending nobody else can see starting.

cells.tense: You still hold what people feel, and it rarely makes its way back out.
cells.ask: Say one true thing out loud to one person today, in your own words.
cells.core:
You still catch the shift in a room, still notice who's carrying something, still keep the space steady without discussing it. What stopped is the part where any of it comes back out of you. It stays inside and reads as calm from the outside, so it passes.

Say one true thing out loud to one person, the plain version. Not the summary, not the version that keeps everything smooth. What you actually noticed, what you actually think. It doesn't have to be tidy and it doesn't have to land well. One true sentence to one person is small, and it counts as the thing starting up again. That's where it starts, anyhow — with words that leave your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You still hold it. Lately it just doesn't come back out.

cells.tense: You are the one keeping this steady, and you speak of it as though it keeps itself.
cells.ask: Write down something you call automatic, then rewrite it starting with "I keep".
cells.core:
You are the one keeping it steady. The timing, the attention, the way a hard moment gets held long enough to pass — that's your doing, not the room's. You describe it as just how things go, and it has gone that way because you keep it going.

Strip the story to plain fact. Somebody noticed something you did this week and you said it was nothing. Take one habit you've been filing under automatic and rewrite that sentence with "I keep" in front of it. Nobody has to read it. This runs whether or not you say so, and saying so is the only part missing. Start small enough that you can't argue with it.

attempts.check: The record gives a balanced face and mechanism for each status but nothing about this person's history, so the draft must not locate what happened behind a stopped offering. The reader could reasonably say the sorting between what's theirs to hold and what isn't was never the problem, and the ask would still be usable because telling one person plainly what's not working right now doesn't depend on my read. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that says what the steadiness has quietly been doing — cut it before the person can call it flattery.
